catalog_quote: In preliminary discussions with Bidya Thoumoung and other Aiton informants in November 1999, five tones were recognised. ... While working through the word list, it became clear that Bidya Thoumoung assigned Tone 5 only to dead or checked syllables, and Tone 3 only to syllables with final nasals or final vowels, and that therefore Tones 3 & 5 were probably allotones of the same toneme. Tone 4 was rarely assigned, and in particular was not assigned to the word for ‘dog’ when that word was encountered in the word list. It therefore appeared that tone 4 was a sporadic allotone of Tone 1. On the basis of this, the following tone box, is proposed for contemporary Aiton (Table 6.68) ... audit.reasoning: The record codes Aiton as 'tonal' with no word-stress rule, resting on Morey 2005, the Pacific Linguistics reference grammar by the language's principal describer; both the deciding tone passage (pp. 161-162) and the domain/vowel-reduction passage (p. 155) are verbatim in the held archive.org text. Glottolog has only one descriptive ref (a 2018 Tezpur masters thesis), so nothing outranks Morey. I fetched sources and scanned Morey's 2005 LTBA article (open, SEAlang), whose Aiton section (pp. 162-165) independently confirms the three-tone analysis and uses 'stressed' only for phrase-level prominence conditioning a rising allotone of Tone 1; Morey 2014 (LD&C, open) is Phake-centred and silent on Aiton stress; Borah 2020 (Shodhganga, Assamese) could not be read. No source seen suggests a word-stress system; wishlist items are low priority corroboration only.

sources.citation: Morey, Stephen. 2005. Tonal change in the Tai languages of Northeast India. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 28.2: 139-202.
sources.quote: 'The Aitons themselves believe that today they speak a language with three tones ... Tones 3 & 5 were probably allotones of the same toneme. Tone 4 ... a sporadic allotone of Tone 1. On the basis of this, the tone box in Table 11 is proposed for contemporary Aiton: 1 mid/high level, 2 high level then falling, 3 mid falling' (pp. 162-163); 'there is an allotone of Tone 1 which is rising ... This most often occurs in stressed positions or at the end of an intonation unit' (p. 163); 'An analysis of Banchob's recordings also confirms a three tone analysis for Aiton' (p. 165).
